notes:
1. Delhi Sultanate — Overview

  • The Delhi Sultanate refers to the series of Muslim dynasties that ruled large parts of northern India from 1206 to 1526 CE.
  • Delhi served as the principal political centre for most of the period.
  • The Sultanate expanded at different times into:
  • Punjab.
  • Ganga-Yamuna plains.
  • Rajasthan.
  • Gujarat.
  • Bengal.
  • Central India.
  • Deccan and parts of South India.
📌 Must-Memorise

Delhi Sultanate → 1206–1526 CE

2. Five Dynasties of Delhi Sultanate

The five major dynasties were:

  • Mamluk or Slave Dynasty → 1206–1290.
  • Khalji Dynasty → 1290–1320.
  • Tughlaq Dynasty → 1320–1414.
  • Sayyid Dynasty → 1414–1451.
  • Lodi Dynasty → 1451–1526.
📌 TNPSC Memory Chain

Slave → Khalji → Tughlaq → Sayyid → Lodi

3. Background — Ghurid Expansion

  • Before the establishment of the Delhi Sultanate, Muhammad of Ghor expanded Ghurid power into northern India.
  • His military victories created the political foundation from which the Delhi Sultanate later emerged.

4. Muhammad of Ghor

  • Muhammad of Ghor is also known as Mu'izz al-Din Muhammad.
  • He defeated important Rajput powers in northern India.
  • He did not establish a hereditary ruling dynasty in India himself.

5. First Battle of Tarain

  • First Battle of Tarain was fought in 1191 CE.
  • Prithviraj Chauhan defeated Muhammad of Ghor.
📌 Must-Memorise

1191 → First Tarain → Prithviraj Victory

6. Second Battle of Tarain

  • Second Battle of Tarain was fought in 1192 CE.
  • Muhammad of Ghor defeated Prithviraj Chauhan.
📌 Must-Memorise

1192 → Second Tarain → Muhammad of Ghor Victory

7. Importance of Second Battle of Tarain

  • The victory opened the way for further Ghurid expansion in northern India.
  • It weakened major Rajput resistance in the Delhi-Ajmer region.

8. Battle of Chandawar

  • Battle of Chandawar was fought in 1194 CE.
  • Muhammad of Ghor defeated Jayachandra of the Gahadavala dynasty.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

1194 → Chandawar → Muhammad of Ghor vs Jayachandra

9. Qutb-ud-din Aibak

  • Qutb-ud-din Aibak was a Turkish slave-general of Muhammad of Ghor.
  • After Muhammad of Ghor's death in 1206, Aibak established independent authority in India.
📌 Must-Memorise

Founder of Delhi Sultanate → Qutb-ud-din Aibak

10. Mamluk / Slave Dynasty

  • The first dynasty of the Delhi Sultanate is commonly called:
  • Mamluk Dynasty.
  • Slave Dynasty.
  • It ruled from 1206 to 1290 CE.

11. Meaning of Mamluk

  • Mamluk refers to a military slave who had been trained for service.
  • Several early rulers rose from slave origins.

12. Qutb-ud-din Aibak — Reign

  • Aibak ruled from 1206 to 1210 CE.
  • His reign was short but important in establishing independent Turkish rule in northern India.

13. Capital of Aibak

  • Aibak initially ruled mainly from Lahore.
  • Delhi also emerged as an important political centre.

14. Lakh Baksh

  • Qutb-ud-din Aibak was known as Lakh Baksh because of his generosity.
📌 Must-Memorise

Lakh Baksh → Qutb-ud-din Aibak

15. Aibak and Architecture

Important monuments associated with Aibak include:

  • Quwwat-ul-Islam Mosque.
  • Beginning of Qutb Minar.
  • Adhai Din ka Jhonpra at Ajmer.

16. Quwwat-ul-Islam Mosque

  • Quwwat-ul-Islam Mosque is located in Delhi.
  • It was constructed after the Turkish conquest of Delhi.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Quwwat-ul-Islam → Aibak → Delhi

17. Qutb Minar

  • Construction of Qutb Minar was begun by Qutb-ud-din Aibak.
  • It was substantially completed by Iltutmish.
  • Later repairs and additions were made by other rulers.
📌 Must-Memorise

Qutb Minar → Begun Aibak → Completed mainly Iltutmish

18. Death of Aibak

  • Qutb-ud-din Aibak died in 1210 CE.
  • He died after falling from a horse while playing chaugan, a form of polo.
📌 Must-Memorise

Aibak → Died Playing Chaugan

19. Aram Shah

  • Aram Shah succeeded Aibak briefly.
  • His claim to succession was weak.
  • He was replaced by Iltutmish.

20. Iltutmish

  • Shams-ud-din Iltutmish became ruler in 1211 CE.
  • He is regarded as the real consolidator of the Delhi Sultanate.
📌 Must-Memorise

Real Consolidator of Delhi Sultanate → Iltutmish

21. Iltutmish and Delhi

  • Iltutmish made Delhi the principal centre of his kingdom.
  • He consolidated Turkish rule across northern India.

22. Major Challenges Faced by Iltutmish

He dealt with:

  • Rival Turkish nobles.
  • Yildiz of Ghazni.
  • Qubacha of Multan and Sind.
  • Rajput resistance.
  • Threat of Mongol expansion.

23. Defeat of Yildiz

  • Iltutmish defeated Taj-ud-din Yildiz.
  • This helped free Delhi from rival claims linked with Ghazni.

24. Qubacha

  • Nasir-ud-din Qubacha controlled Multan and Sind.
  • Iltutmish defeated him and expanded his authority in the northwest.

25. Mongol Threat

  • During Iltutmish's reign, Genghis Khan reached the Indus region while pursuing Jalal-ud-din Mangburni.
  • Iltutmish avoided direct confrontation with the Mongols.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Iltutmish → Avoided Conflict with Genghis Khan

26. Caliphal Recognition

  • In 1229 CE, Iltutmish received formal recognition from the Abbasid Caliph.
  • This strengthened his political legitimacy.
📌 Must-Memorise

1229 → Caliph Recognised Iltutmish

27. Iltutmish and Coinage

Iltutmish introduced important coinage:

  • Silver tanka.
  • Copper jital.
📌 Must-Memorise

Iltutmish → Silver Tanka + Copper Jital

28. Tanka

  • Tanka became an important silver coin of the Delhi Sultanate.

29. Jital

  • Jital was a lower-value copper coin used widely.

30. Iqta System

  • Iltutmish helped organise the iqta system in the Delhi Sultanate.
  • Iqtas were assignments of revenue from territories to officials in return for service.
📌 Must-Memorise

Iqta → Revenue Assignment

31. Iqtadar / Muqti

  • The holder of an iqta was called:
  • Iqtadar.
  • Muqti.
  • He collected revenue and maintained troops and administration in the assigned territory.

32. Iqta Was Not Absolute Ownership

  • An iqta was essentially a revenue assignment, not unrestricted hereditary private ownership of land.
  • The Sultan could transfer officials from one iqta to another.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Iqta ≠ Permanent Private Land Ownership

33. Turkan-i-Chahalgani

  • Iltutmish organised a group of powerful Turkish nobles known as the Chahalgani or Corps of Forty.
📌 Must-Memorise

Chahalgani / Forty → Iltutmish

34. Meaning of Chahalgani

  • Chahalgani literally refers to a group of forty.
  • It represented elite Turkish nobles who became very influential in politics.

35. Iltutmish and Qutb Minar

  • Iltutmish added important storeys to the Qutb Minar.
  • He also constructed major buildings around the Qutb complex.

36. Tomb of Iltutmish

  • Iltutmish's tomb is located in the Qutb complex at Delhi.
  • It is an important early Indo-Islamic monument.

37. Razia Sultan

  • Razia succeeded Iltutmish in 1236 CE.
  • She ruled from 1236 to 1240 CE.
  • She was the first and only woman to rule the Delhi Sultanate in her own right.
📌 Must-Memorise

Razia Sultan → 1236–1240 → First Woman Sultan of Delhi

38. Iltutmish and Razia

  • Iltutmish considered Razia capable of succession.
  • Her rule faced resistance from powerful Turkish nobles.

39. Title of Razia

  • Razia preferred the title Sultan rather than merely Sultana.
  • She attempted to exercise sovereign authority independently.

40. Razia's Political Challenge

She faced opposition from:

  • Turkish nobles.
  • Provincial governors.
  • Court factions.

41. Jamal-ud-din Yaqut

  • Yaqut was an Abyssinian officer associated with Razia's court.
  • His rise contributed to hostility among Turkish nobles.

42. Malik Altunia

  • Malik Altunia was governor of Bhatinda.
  • He rebelled against Razia.
  • Razia later married him.

43. Death of Razia

  • Razia was defeated and killed in 1240 CE.
  • Her short reign demonstrated the power of the Turkish nobility.

44. Later Slave Rulers

After Razia, the Sultanate experienced instability under rulers including:

  • Bahram Shah.
  • Masud Shah.
  • Nasir-ud-din Mahmud.

45. Nasir-ud-din Mahmud

  • Nasir-ud-din Mahmud ruled from 1246 to 1266 CE.
  • Much real political power was exercised by Balban.

46. Ghiyas-ud-din Balban

  • Balban became Sultan in 1266 CE.
  • He strengthened royal authority and suppressed powerful nobles and rebels.
📌 Must-Memorise

Balban → Strong Monarchy

47. Balban's Theory of Kingship

Balban emphasised:

  • Divine prestige of kingship.
  • Absolute authority.
  • Court discipline.
  • Distance between ruler and ordinary people.

48. Zill-i-Ilahi

  • Balban promoted the idea of the Sultan as Zill-i-Ilahi, or shadow of God on Earth.
📌 Must-Memorise

Zill-i-Ilahi → Balban

49. Niyabat-i-Khudai

  • Balban also emphasised the king as God's representative or deputy.
  • This elevated the political status of the Sultan.

50. Sijda and Paibos

Balban introduced or strongly enforced court practices such as:

  • Sijda → Prostration before the ruler.
  • Paibos → Kissing the ruler's feet.
📌 Must-Memorise

Balban → Sijda + Paibos

51. Blood and Iron Policy

  • Balban followed a severe policy against rebellion and disorder.
  • It is often described as a policy of "Blood and Iron."
📌 Must-Memorise

Blood and Iron → Balban

52. Destruction of Chahalgani Power

  • Balban reduced the power of the Corps of Forty.
  • He sought to prevent nobles from challenging royal authority.

53. Balban and Mongols

  • Balban strengthened the northwestern frontier against Mongol raids.
  • Frontier fortifications and military preparations were improved.

54. Balban and Mewatis

  • Balban suppressed Mewati raiders around Delhi.
  • Forests were cleared and military posts established in affected areas.

55. Balban's Son Muhammad

  • Prince Muhammad, Balban's son, was killed fighting the Mongols.
  • The death deeply affected Balban.

56. End of Slave Dynasty

  • After Balban's death in 1287, political instability increased.
  • The dynasty ended in 1290 with the rise of the Khaljis.

57. Khalji Dynasty

  • The Khalji Dynasty ruled from 1290 to 1320 CE.
  • It was founded by Jalal-ud-din Firuz Khalji.
📌 Must-Memorise

Khalji Dynasty → 1290–1320

58. Jalal-ud-din Firuz Khalji

  • Jalal-ud-din Khalji founded the dynasty in 1290 CE.
  • He adopted a comparatively mild political approach.
  • He was later killed by his nephew and son-in-law Alauddin Khalji.

59. Alauddin Khalji

  • Alauddin Khalji became Sultan in 1296 CE.
  • He was one of the most powerful rulers of the Delhi Sultanate.
📌 Must-Memorise

Alauddin Khalji → 1296–1316

60. Alauddin's Early Campaign

  • Before becoming Sultan, Alauddin led a raid on Devagiri.
  • The wealth obtained strengthened his political position.

61. Devagiri

  • Devagiri was the capital of the Yadava kingdom.
  • It was located in the Deccan.
  • It later became known as Daulatabad.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Devagiri → Yadavas → Later Daulatabad

62. Alauddin's Northern Conquests

He conquered or subdued:

  • Gujarat.
  • Ranthambore.
  • Chittor.
  • Malwa.
  • Jalore.

63. Gujarat Campaign

  • Gujarat was conquered by Alauddin's forces.
  • The campaign brought wealth and access to western trade centres.

64. Ranthambore

  • Alauddin captured Ranthambore in 1301 CE.
  • The fort was an important Rajput stronghold.

65. Chittor

  • Alauddin captured Chittor in 1303 CE.
  • Chittor was a major fort of Mewar.
📌 Must-Memorise

Chittor Conquest → Alauddin Khalji → 1303

66. Alauddin and Mongols

  • Alauddin faced several Mongol invasions.
  • He strengthened frontier defence and maintained a large standing army.

67. Siri

  • Alauddin Khalji built the city of Siri near Delhi.
  • It became an important military and administrative centre.
📌 Must-Memorise

Siri City → Alauddin Khalji

68. Southern Expeditions

Alauddin's forces expanded influence into South India under Malik Kafur.

Major targets included:

  • Devagiri.
  • Warangal.
  • Dwarasamudra.
  • Madurai/Pandya country.

69. Malik Kafur

  • Malik Kafur was a prominent general of Alauddin Khalji.
  • He led major expeditions into the Deccan and South India.
📌 Must-Memorise

Malik Kafur → Alauddin's Southern Campaigns

70. Warangal Campaign

  • Malik Kafur attacked Warangal.
  • Warangal was ruled by the Kakatiyas.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Warangal → Kakatiya Dynasty

71. Prataparudra II

  • Kakatiya ruler Prataparudra II submitted and paid tribute after Khalji campaigns.

72. Dwarasamudra

  • Dwarasamudra was the capital of the Hoysala kingdom.
  • It is associated with present-day Halebidu in Karnataka.
📌 Must-Memorise

Dwarasamudra → Hoysalas

73. Hoysala Ruler

  • Veera Ballala III was the important Hoysala ruler during this period.
  • He accepted tributary arrangements after Khalji pressure.

74. Pandya Country

  • Malik Kafur's forces entered the Pandya kingdom in the far south.
  • Political conflict within the Pandya kingdom facilitated the invasion.
📌 Tamil Nadu Must-Memorise

Malik Kafur → Pandya Country → South India

75. Madurai Campaign

  • Khalji forces raided the Madurai region and acquired substantial wealth.
  • Delhi did not immediately establish durable direct administration over the entire Tamil region during Alauddin's reign.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Malik Kafur's Raid ≠ Immediate Permanent Delhi Rule Over All Tamil Nadu

76. Alauddin's Imperial Policy

  • Southern kingdoms were often required to:
  • Pay tribute.
  • Accept political subordination.
  • Direct annexation was limited in distant southern regions.

77. Alauddin's Administrative Reforms

Alauddin introduced major reforms in:

  • Military administration.
  • Revenue collection.
  • Market regulation.
  • Intelligence.
  • Control of nobles.

78. Market Reforms

  • Alauddin introduced strict price controls in Delhi.
  • The purpose was closely connected with maintaining a large army at relatively low cost.
📌 Must-Memorise

Price Control → Alauddin Khalji

79. Markets Under Alauddin

Separate markets were regulated for:

  • Grain.
  • Cloth and daily necessities.
  • Horses.
  • Slaves and cattle.

80. Diwan-i-Riyasat

  • Diwan-i-Riyasat was an important department associated with market control.
📌 Must-Memorise

Diwan-i-Riyasat → Market Regulation

81. Shahna-i-Mandi

  • Shahna-i-Mandi was an official responsible for supervising markets.
📌 Must-Memorise

Shahna-i-Mandi → Market Superintendent

82. Grain Regulation

  • Grain prices were fixed.
  • State granaries and regulated supplies were used to stabilise markets.

83. Intelligence Network

  • Alauddin maintained an extensive spy system.
  • Officials monitored:
  • Nobles.
  • Markets.
  • Military affairs.

84. Barid

  • Barids acted as intelligence and reporting officials.

85. Munhiyan

  • Munhiyans were secret informers used to report violations and political activity.

86. Control of Nobles

Alauddin restricted:

  • Social gatherings.
  • Drinking parties.
  • Marriage alliances among nobles without approval.
  • Accumulation of excessive wealth.

87. Revenue Reform

  • Alauddin increased state control over land revenue in the Doab and other core areas.
  • Land was measured in some regions.
  • Revenue demand was very high.

88. Kharaj

  • Kharaj referred to land revenue or agricultural tax.

89. Revenue Demand

  • In some core agricultural regions, the state demand is described as reaching about half of agricultural produce.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Alauddin → Heavy Land Revenue Demand

90. Ghari and Charai

Alauddin imposed taxes such as:

  • Ghari → House tax.
  • Charai → Grazing tax.
📌 Must-Memorise

Ghari → House Tax

Charai → Grazing Tax

91. Military Reform

Alauddin introduced:

  • Dagh.
  • Chehra.
📌 Must-Memorise

Dagh + Chehra → Alauddin Khalji

92. Dagh

  • Dagh referred to branding of horses.
  • It prevented substitution of inferior horses.

93. Chehra

  • Chehra referred to descriptive rolls or identification records of soldiers.

94. Standing Army

  • Alauddin maintained a large centrally paid standing army.
  • Market controls helped reduce the cost of maintaining this force.

95. Alauddin and Ulema

  • Alauddin asserted strong state authority.
  • He did not allow religious scholars to fully dictate political policy.

96. Architecture of Alauddin

Important works include:

  • Siri Fort.
  • Alai Darwaza.
  • Hauz-i-Alai, later known as Hauz Khas.
  • Beginning of Alai Minar.

97. Alai Darwaza

  • Alai Darwaza was built by Alauddin Khalji.
  • It is an important example of early Indo-Islamic architecture using:
  • True arch.
  • Dome.
  • Decorative stonework.
📌 Must-Memorise

Alai Darwaza → Alauddin Khalji

98. Alai Minar

  • Alauddin planned the Alai Minar to be larger than Qutb Minar.
  • It remained unfinished.

99. Amir Khusrau

  • Amir Khusrau was a major Persian poet, writer and musician associated with several Delhi Sultans.
  • He lived during the late Slave and Khalji periods.
📌 Must-Memorise

Amir Khusrau → Delhi Sultanate Court Poet

100. Titles of Amir Khusrau

  • Amir Khusrau is often called:
  • Tuti-i-Hind.
  • Parrot of India.
📌 Must-Memorise

Tuti-i-Hind → Amir Khusrau

101. Amir Khusrau and Alauddin

  • Amir Khusrau wrote important works on Alauddin's reign and military achievements.
  • Khazain-ul-Futuh is particularly associated with Alauddin's conquests.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Khazain-ul-Futuh → Amir Khusrau → Alauddin Khalji

102. Khazain-ul-Futuh

  • Also known as Tarikh-i-Alai.
  • It describes many achievements of Alauddin Khalji.

103. End of Khalji Dynasty

  • Alauddin died in 1316.
  • Political instability followed.
  • The dynasty ended in 1320.

104. Tughlaq Dynasty

  • Tughlaq Dynasty ruled from 1320 to 1414 CE.
  • It was founded by Ghiyas-ud-din Tughlaq.
📌 Must-Memorise

Tughlaq Dynasty → 1320–1414

105. Ghiyas-ud-din Tughlaq

  • Ghiyas-ud-din Tughlaq founded the dynasty in 1320.
  • He had earlier served as a frontier commander.

106. Tughlaqabad

  • Ghiyas-ud-din Tughlaq built Tughlaqabad near Delhi.
  • It is known for massive fortified architecture.
📌 Must-Memorise

Tughlaqabad → Ghiyas-ud-din Tughlaq

107. Tomb of Ghiyas-ud-din

  • His tomb is a major example of early Tughlaq architecture.
  • It features:
  • Sloping walls.
  • Strong fortress-like appearance.

108. Death of Ghiyas-ud-din

  • Ghiyas-ud-din died in 1325 after the collapse of a pavilion.
  • Muhammad bin Tughlaq succeeded him.

109. Muhammad bin Tughlaq

  • Muhammad bin Tughlaq ruled from 1325 to 1351 CE.
  • He was highly educated and ambitious.
  • His reign is famous for bold but often unsuccessful experiments.
📌 Must-Memorise

Muhammad bin Tughlaq → 1325–1351

110. Major Experiments of Muhammad bin Tughlaq

Important policies included:

  • Transfer of capital.
  • Token currency.
  • Increased taxation in the Doab.
  • Agricultural development schemes.
  • Large military ambitions.

111. Transfer of Capital

  • Muhammad bin Tughlaq ordered transfer of the capital from Delhi to Devagiri.
  • Devagiri was renamed Daulatabad.
📌 Must-Memorise

Delhi → Daulatabad → Muhammad bin Tughlaq

112. Reason for Daulatabad

Possible reasons included:

  • More central geographical location.
  • Better control over the Deccan.
  • Security considerations.

Historians debate his precise motivations.

113. Problems of Capital Transfer

  • Large-scale movement caused hardship.
  • The policy was eventually reversed.
  • Delhi again became the main capital.

114. Token Currency

  • Muhammad bin Tughlaq introduced token currency using base metals.
  • Copper or brass coins were intended to circulate at values comparable to precious-metal currency.
📌 Must-Memorise

Token Currency → Muhammad bin Tughlaq

115. Failure of Token Currency

Major problems included:

  • Widespread counterfeiting.
  • Lack of effective state monopoly over coin production.
  • Loss of public confidence.

116. Withdrawal of Token Currency

  • The Sultan eventually withdrew the experiment.
  • Counterfeit token coins could be exchanged for precious-metal currency, causing heavy financial losses.

117. Doab Taxation

  • Muhammad bin Tughlaq increased taxation in the Ganga-Yamuna Doab.
  • The policy coincided with agricultural distress and created severe hardship.

118. Doab

  • Doab means land between two rivers.
  • In this context it refers especially to the Ganga-Yamuna Doab.
📌 Must-Memorise

Doab → Land Between Two Rivers

119. Diwan-i-Kohi

  • Muhammad bin Tughlaq established Diwan-i-Kohi for agricultural development.
📌 Must-Memorise

Diwan-i-Kohi → Agriculture → Muhammad bin Tughlaq

120. Agricultural Experiment

  • Loans were provided to cultivators.
  • The aim was to bring uncultivated land under cultivation.
  • Poor implementation limited success.

121. Qarachil Expedition

  • Muhammad bin Tughlaq launched an expedition into the Himalayan region.
  • It ended disastrously for his army.

122. Khurasan Project

  • Muhammad bin Tughlaq planned a major expedition toward Khurasan.
  • A large army was prepared.
  • The expedition was ultimately abandoned.

123. Ibn Battuta

  • Moroccan traveller Ibn Battuta visited India during Muhammad bin Tughlaq's reign.
  • He arrived in India in the 1330s.
📌 Must-Memorise

Ibn Battuta → Muhammad bin Tughlaq

124. Ibn Battuta's Book

  • His travel account is known as Rihla.
📌 Must-Memorise

Rihla → Ibn Battuta

125. Ibn Battuta as Qazi

  • Muhammad bin Tughlaq appointed Ibn Battuta as a qazi in Delhi.

126. Ibn Battuta's Observations

His account provides information on:

  • Court life.
  • Roads.
  • Postal system.
  • Cities.
  • Slavery.
  • Social practices.
  • Trade.

127. Postal System

  • Ibn Battuta described a highly developed relay postal system.
  • Messages and goods could move rapidly across long distances.

128. Expansion Under Muhammad bin Tughlaq

  • His empire briefly reached one of the widest territorial extents of the Delhi Sultanate.
  • Maintaining control over distant regions proved difficult.

129. Rebellions

During his reign, many regions rebelled.

Important consequences included emergence of:

  • Vijayanagara Empire.
  • Bahmani Sultanate.
  • Independent provincial states.

130. Vijayanagara Foundation

  • Vijayanagara Empire was founded in 1336.
  • Harihara and Bukka were its founders.
🔗 South India Key Link

1336 → Vijayanagara → Harihara and Bukka

131. Bahmani Sultanate

  • Bahmani Sultanate was established in 1347.
  • It emerged in the Deccan after breaking away from Delhi authority.
📌 Must-Memorise

1347 → Bahmani Sultanate

132. Madurai Sultanate

  • A short-lived independent Sultanate emerged at Madurai during the weakening of Delhi authority in the south.
  • It existed during the 14th century.
🔗 Tamil Nadu Key Link

Madurai Sultanate → 14th Century → Post-Tughlaq Fragmentation

133. Madurai Sultanate and Pandya Decline

  • Political instability after Pandya decline and northern military interventions facilitated the formation of the Madurai Sultanate.

134. Muhammad bin Tughlaq — Assessment

  • He was intellectually capable and ambitious.
  • Several policies failed because of:
  • Poor implementation.
  • Administrative limitations.
  • Geographic overextension.
  • Resistance.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Muhammad bin Tughlaq → Not Simply "Mad"; Policies Had Rational Aims but Often Failed

135. Firuz Shah Tughlaq

  • Firuz Shah Tughlaq ruled from 1351 to 1388 CE.
  • His approach differed greatly from Muhammad bin Tughlaq.
📌 Must-Memorise

Firuz Shah Tughlaq → 1351–1388

136. Firuz Shah's Policy

He focused on:

  • Irrigation.
  • Public works.
  • Revenue administration.
  • Religious orthodoxy.
  • Hereditary appointments.

137. Irrigation Works

  • Firuz Shah constructed and repaired canals.
  • Irrigation expanded agriculture in parts of northern India.
📌 Must-Memorise

Canal Construction → Firuz Shah Tughlaq

138. Canals of Firuz Shah

Canals connected or drew water from rivers such as:

  • Yamuna.
  • Sutlej.
  • Ghaggar.

139. Firuzabad

  • Firuz Shah established Firuzabad as a new city near Delhi.

140. Firoz Shah Kotla

  • Firoz Shah Kotla was built by Firuz Shah Tughlaq.
  • It became an important palace-fort complex.
📌 Must-Memorise

Firoz Shah Kotla → Firuz Shah Tughlaq

141. Ashokan Pillars

  • Firuz Shah transported Ashokan pillars to Delhi.
  • One was brought from Topra.
  • Another came from Meerut.
📌 Must-Memorise

Ashokan Pillars Transported to Delhi → Firuz Shah Tughlaq

142. Diwan-i-Khairat

  • Firuz Shah established Diwan-i-Khairat for charitable purposes.
📌 Must-Memorise

Diwan-i-Khairat → Charity → Firuz Shah

143. Dar-ul-Shifa

  • Dar-ul-Shifa referred to a charitable hospital or medical institution associated with Firuz's welfare measures.

144. Diwan-i-Bandagan

  • Firuz Shah maintained a department associated with slaves known as Diwan-i-Bandagan.
